MLCB MINA Spotlight

PaperPoster (PDF)

01

Speaker notes

DNA language models are now a standard feature extractor, but do frozen embeddings know more than counting nucleotides and amino acids?

We take a gene's coding sequence, chunk it, and run each chunk through a frozen DNA encoder: DNABERT-2, NT-v2, GENA-LM, or HyenaDNA.
02

Speaker notes

That gives one vector per chunk. We then aggregate them with different pooling rules (mean, max, CLS token, or chunk ends), which collapses them into one gene vector.
03

Speaker notes

Then we evaluate this vector with a linear probe on two tasks: (1) predicting the gene family, and (2) predicting the text description of the gene by mapping it to GenePT's text embedding, scored by R².
04

Speaker notes

Then we split genes by protein clusters, so there is no leakage between train and test.
05

Speaker notes

And we used counting baselines: nucleotide k-mers and, after translating to protein, amino-acid k-mers. The protein model ESM-2 is a reference ceiling.
06

Speaker notes

On protein family, the DNA encoders are not significantly above the 6-mer, and no encoder reaches amino-acid counts. The text task tells the same story. Frozen DNA encoders sit at composition level.
07

Speaker notes

However, it turns out that evaluation choices matter as much as, or even more than, encoder choice.

For reference, switching encoders gives us a range of 0.08.
08

Speaker notes

Input region matters a lot: switching the input from the CDS to a TSS window, which is mostly introns, drops macro-F1 from 0.69 to 0.30.
09

Speaker notes

Pooling matters a lot too: with the same embeddings, max pooling gives 0.50, which is worse than the 6-mer; the best mean rule gives 0.70.
10

Speaker notes

Split: a random split leaks near-copies into test. NT-v2 inflates from 0.69 to 0.80, and amino-acid counts inflate even more, to 0.91, but the ranking holds.
11

Speaker notes

So evaluation choices move scores as much as the encoder does, often more. When you probe a DNA model, compare against composition baselines, use the coding sequence, split by homology, and pick pooling on validation.

Come see us at poster 40. Thank you.
